analysis.one_liner: Bans seismic airgun blasting for offshore oil and gas exploration in the Atlantic.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate vote; it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee from May 2017 until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit oil, gas, and methane hydrate exploration activities — including seismic airgun blasting, which fires loud sound pulses at the ocean floor to map oil and gas deposits — in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2] [S3]. Seismic surveys are the first step toward offshore drilling; the bill would have blocked that step for the entire Atlantic coast. It was introduced by Senator Booker with twelve cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it received no further action [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities whose economies depend on fishing and tourism, commercial fishermen whose catch depends on healthy fish populations, and marine wildlife, especially whales and dolphins whose hearing and communication would be damaged by repeated airgun blasts.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person or federal agency from conducting geological or geophysical activities in support of oil, gas, or methane hydrate exploration and development in the four Atlantic planning areas of the outer Continental Shelf [S3].
Seismic airgun surveys fire intense sound pulses toward the ocean floor, and the bill would have stopped them before any Atlantic exploration program could begin [S2] [S3].

Because seismic surveys are the prerequisite for offshore leasing and drilling, the moratorium would have kept the Atlantic coast out of the exploration pipeline during the period the ban applied [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and seismic survey contractors, who would lose access to the Atlantic outer Continental Shelf for exploration, and potentially energy consumers to the extent Atlantic resources go undeveloped.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers exploration surveys, not drilling itself, so it does not by itself stop offshore drilling — it removes the mapping step, which critics said would leave the government and industry without data even for decisions about whether development makes sense [S2] [S3].

A blanket statutory prohibition forecloses resource assessment for the entire Atlantic coast, including any future balance between energy development and environmental protection that Congress might prefer to strike through normal leasing procedures rather than a moratorium [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Atlantic coastal states, the benefits — protected fisheries, marine mammal populations, and tourism economies — are local and ongoing, while the costs fall mainly on exploration companies and on potential future energy supply. The bill's main design weakness is that a flat statutory moratorium, rather than the ordinary environmental review and leasing process, is a blunt instrument: it applies regardless of what future surveys might find. The core tradeoff is straightforward: keeping seismic blasting out of the Atlantic versus keeping exploration options open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on May 25, 2017, with Senators Whitehouse, Nelson, Blumenthal, Menendez, Cardin, Markey, Hassan, Warren, Shaheen, and Sanders as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources; that is the last action recorded in the 115th Congress [S5].
It had 12 cosponsors, 11 Democrats and 1 Independent, and no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas and seismic survey companies kept Atlantic waters open to exploration, and no restrictions were placed on airgun blasting during the Congress; coastal fishing and tourism interests remained without the protection the bill would have provided.

against.what_they_did: The committee she chaired never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without any action after its referral.

against.name: Trump administration Interior Department
against.what_they_did: Pushed in the opposite direction, proposing offshore drilling in the Atlantic and advancing seismic survey permitting, which the bill would have prohibited.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders, and with the Energy and Natural Resources Committee chaired by a Republican the bill never moved [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Seismic survey and offshore oil and gas exploration companies
industries.note: The bill would have prohibited their core activity — airgun surveys to map Atlantic oil and gas deposits — cutting them off from the Atlantic outer Continental Shelf [S2] [S3]. Their interest in running loud surveys off the coast runs against coastal fishing and tourism economies that depend on healthy marine life [S2].
Airgun blasting disrupts fish populations and marine mammals that fisheries depend on; banning the surveys protects the resource on which fishing livelihoods rest [S2].
Beach and coastal economies depend on healthy oceans and marine wildlife, which repeated seismic blasting would degrade; the bill keeps that threat off the Atlantic coast [S2].
